title: Lynxes Caught Soaking Their Prey—A Carnivore First That Hints at Hidden Smarts
summary: When a camera trap in central Spain captured a female Iberian lynx carrying a dead rabbit to a water trough and deliberately submerging it, researchers were stunned. Carnivores simply don't do that. Yet between 2020 and 2025, scientists documented eight instances of this unprecedented behavior among five different lynxes in the Montes de Toledo mountain range. Each time, the cat soaked the rabbit for about a minute—one dunk lasted over four minutes—before carrying it away uneaten. Published in Ecology, the findings mark the first-ever observation of a carnivore soaking its prey in water. "This is genuinely a surprising observation," says Wai-Ming Wong, director of small-cat conservation science for Panthera. "Wild cats are typically thought of as highly efficient, instinct-driven hunters, so seeing an individual modify how it handles prey in this way is quite remarkable." The Iberian lynx (Lynx pardinus) is a specialized predator that depends on European rabbits for at least 80% of its diet. The species was on the brink of extinction—fewer than 100 individuals remained in 2002—but conservation efforts have boosted numbers to around 2,401. The soaking behavior emerged only after years of monitoring. Researchers ruled out extreme heat as a trigger. Instead, they noticed that all the soaking lynxes were female and of reproductive age, and that the behavior occurred within overlapping territories or among descendants. This pattern suggests the trait spread through kin-based social networks, even though lynxes are generally solitary. "Although lynx are generally solitary, they exhibit a certain degree of social cohesion that is largely kin‑based," notes lead author José Jiménez of the Spanish National Research Council. The leading hypothesis is maternal care. Female lynxes raise cubs alone, and the researchers propose that soaking prey adds hydration and softens the meat, easing the cubs' transition from milk to solid food. Lab tests showed a rabbit carcass soaked for 30 seconds retained nearly 4% of its body weight in water 40 minutes later. Wong agrees the behavior is likely learned, not instinctive. "Most evidence suggests these kinds of behaviors would be learned rather than instinctive, perhaps often starting with a single individual experimenting, accidentally at first, and then repeating the behavior because it provides some benefit." The discovery underscores the cognitive sophistication of wild felids and their capacity to adapt to changing environments—a crucial trait as the lynx's Mediterranean forest habitat faces fragmentation from development and agriculture, and rabbit populations fluctuate due to disease and hunting.
why_it_matters: This discovery reshapes how we think about animal intelligence and the importance of family learning in supposedly solitary creatures. For a critically endangered species, such behavioral flexibility might be key to surviving habitat loss and prey shortages—insights that are vital as young people grow into the generation that will need to protect biodiversity.

background_read: The Iberian lynx (Lynx pardinus) is one of the world's rarest wild cats, native only to Spain and Portugal. By 2002 its population had crashed to fewer than 100 individuals due to habitat destruction and a steep decline in European rabbits, its main food source. Since then, intensive conservation work, including captive breeding and reintroduction, has helped numbers climb to around 2,401.

The Montes de Toledo mountain range in central Spain, where the soaking behavior was observed, is a rugged region of Mediterranean scrubland that provides ideal shelter for lynxes. José Jiménez, the lead researcher behind this study, works at the Spanish National Research Council (CSIC), Spain's largest public scientific institution.

Panthera, the organization whose conservation scientist is quoted in the article, is a global nonprofit dedicated exclusively to protecting wild cat species and their habitats. The discovery that a carnivore deliberately modifies how it handles prey challenges long-held ideas about instinct-driven hunting and highlights the hidden intelligence of solitary predators.

├─ QUOTE: Conservation scientist Wai-Ming Wong calls it ‘surprising’
└─ CONTEXT: Iberian lynx is a specialized rabbit predator, once nearly extinct
PATTERN: Soaking only done by females of reproductive age, linked by kinship
└─ SOCIAL LEARNING: Behavior likely spread through kin-based networks despite solitary nature
HYPOTHESIS: Maternal care—soaking adds moisture and softens meat for cubs

└─ LEARNING: Wong suggests the behavior is learned, not purely instinctive
BROADER IMPACT: Discovery reveals cognitive sophistication in wild felids
└─ ECOLOGICAL WORRY: Habitat fragmentation and rabbit declines threaten the lynx's future

perspectives.perspective: Positive: conservation success and cognitive insight
perspectives.description: The observation shows that endangered species can develop clever behavioral adaptations, giving hope for their survival. The fact that the Iberian lynx bounced back from the brink of extinction—and is now revealing hidden social learning—reinforces why conservation programs matter. It also opens a new window into how predator intelligence can help species cope with changing environments.

perspectives.perspective: Negative / critical: limited evidence and possible misinterpretation
perspectives.description: Only a handful of adult female lynxes were seen soaking prey, so the behavior might be rare or situational, not a widespread adaptation. Some scientists may argue that the water gain is too small to really benefit cubs, and the link to maternal care remains a hypothesis. Overstating this finding could divert attention from the pressing threats of habitat loss and rabbit disease.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral / analytical: a piece in the puzzle of animal culture
perspectives.description: This fits into a growing body of research showing that many non-human animals pass on learned behaviors through family lines, a form of rudimentary ‘culture’. Solitary carnivores have long been thought to rely mainly on instinct, but evidence of kin-based social learning challenges that assumption. From an evolutionary perspective, such flexibility may be an underappreciated survival tool.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking: next steps in research and conservation
perspectives.description: Researchers now want to see if the behavior spreads further or if cubs raised by soaking mothers adopt it themselves. If confirmed, conservation programs could consider family structures when reintroducing lynxes to the wild, keeping related females together to preserve local knowledge. Long term, protecting the rabbit population and Mediterranean forests remains the foundation for any behavioral advantage to pay off.
